blocks.html: A pretext of marriage it truly was, for of lawful conjunction, Martin Guerre being alive, there could be none a: for several reasons, of which there are two principal ones. The first, that a woman cannot have two husbands b; nay, it is not credible that she should desire them c, unless it were in the country of the Medes, where the women are brought up in such an opinion that nothing more fortunate or honourable can befall them than for each to have several husbands: indeed, to have fewer than five seems to them a thing as it were ignominious, calamitous and wretched d. The second reason, that although there might have been a marriage, there was error in the person, which error hinders the will, and in consequence the marriage e, which takes its essence from the will and consent of the parties f. It will perhaps be objected to me that between Jacob and Leah there was a marriage, although Jacob thought to espouse and lie with Rachel, for whom he had served Laban his father-in-law seven years — who nevertheless, on the wedding night, substituted for Jacob his elder daughter Leah in place of Rachel the younger g. But the answer is plain: that although at the beginning Jacob had not consented to Leah, nevertheless afterwards he received her as his wife, approving the substitution and the marriage, which suffices h.

notes.citation: Decretum of Gratian, Part II, C. 34 q. 1 (the causa on the wife of a man taken captive who marries again), c. Cum in captivitate (chapter not verified)
notes.original: c. cum in captiuitate. xxxiiij. q j.
notes.gloss: The transcribers read priuitate/ptiuitate for the second half of the word divided across two margin lines; captiuitate either way. The same chapter is cited at annot-094 {d} as c. in captiuitate. Cited for the rule that no second marriage can stand while the first husband lives.
The paragraph contains the rule eadem duobus nupta esse non potest — the same woman cannot be married to two men; the swash P of the print is the paragraph sign.

notes.citation: Digest 23.3 (De iure dotium), the second law beginning Si mulier (fragment not identified)
notes.original: l. ſi mulier. la ij. D. de iur. dot.
notes.gloss: Several fragments of the title open Si mulier; Coras specifies "the second". The transcribers' iur- / iur. is the abbreviation iur[e], read with its point.

notes.original: Strabo au liure xi. de ſa Geographie.
notes.gloss: Strabo on the mountain peoples of Media: it is held honourable for a woman to have as many husbands as possible, and to have fewer than five is thought a calamity.

notes.citation: Decretum, C. 29 q. 1, c. 1 (Gratian's dictum on error of person)
notes.gloss: Error as to the person prevents consent and so the marriage; cited again at annot-097 {q} as c. j. § quod autem, xxix. q. j., and at annot-010 {h}.

notes.citation: Digest 50.17 (De diversis regulis iuris antiqui), l. Nuptias (D. 50.17.30, Ulpian); Decretum, C. 27 q. 2, c. Sufficiat (c. 2)
notes.original: l. nuptias. D. de reg. iur. c. ſufficiat. xxvij. q. ij.
notes.gloss: Nuptias non concubitus, sed consensus facit — it is consent, not intercourse, that makes a marriage; the canon (from Chrysostom) says the consent of the parties alone suffices according to the laws.
Laban substitutes Leah for Rachel. Chapter 27 is the deception of Isaac; the Jacob and Leah story is chapter 29, as the print itself has it at annot-081 {h} and annot-097 {ſ}.

notes.citation: Decretum, C. 30 q. 5, c. Nec illud, at the end (chapter not verified); and C. 29 q. 1, c. 1, cited above at {e}
notes.original: c. nec illud P. ſi. xxx. q. v. & au c. i. preallegué.
